The Polling Problem, and What a WebSocket Is

Every HTTP request is the client asking first — a WebSocket is one connection either side can push through, at any moment, with no request to answer.

Every request this project has handled so far, since Week 1, has the same shape: the client sends a request, the server sends back one response, and the connection's job is done. That shape has no way for the server to speak first. If a customer's browser is sitting on a ticket's page and an agent comments on it in another tab, nothing about a request/response cycle lets the server say "a comment just arrived" — the browser would have to keep asking, over and over, "anything new yet? anything new yet?" (polling) just to find out, most of those requests coming back with nothing to report.

A WebSocket is a different kind of connection, not just a different kind of request: the client opens one connection to the server, and — unlike HTTP — that connection stays open, with both sides able to send a message across it at any moment, in either direction, with no request needing to come first. The server can push "a comment just arrived" the instant that comment is created, because the same open connection is still sitting there waiting for it to send anything, whether or not the client asked. That's the one property polling can't get without either wasting requests or accepting a delay — and it's exactly what this lesson's realtime channel needs: ticket.commented fires once, on the server, and a browser watching that ticket should find out immediately, not on its next poll.
